claims.text: Adding a minor concentration of boron to a phosphorus-containing high-entropy or compositionally complex alloy improves its glass-forming ability.
Adding a minor concentration of boron to such an alloy improves the thermal stability of its amorphous state.
An effective boron addition is expected to be on the order of a few atomic percent.
The beneficial effect occurs only within a limited compositional window.
Homogeneous boron distribution without formation of secondary phases is required for the intervention to be most effective.
Boron atoms preferentially interact with phosphorus.
The boron–phosphorus interaction produces localized strong P–B bonds.
Localized P–B bonding disrupts the formation and growth of short-to-medium-range crystalline clusters.
P–B bond formation locally alters atomic mobility.
P–B bond formation reduces the driving force for phase separation.
The proposed changes in atomic mobility and phase-separation tendency inhibit crystal nucleation and growth during cooling.
Relative to the boron-free baseline, the boron-alloyed specimen will have a lower critical cooling rate for glass formation.
Relative to the boron-free baseline, the boron-alloyed specimen will have a higher crystallization onset temperature.
Excessive boron can cause secondary phases or boride precipitates to form.
Secondary-phase or boride formation can diminish or reverse the proposed benefits of boron addition.
The intervention is limited to compositions in which phosphorus is a significant component and interacts effectively with boron.
